subject: Mathematics
title: Raj's Railway Ticket Mystery
hook: Raj discovers that numbers hide deep secrets at a railway station.

image.alt: Real Numbers: Order and Divisibility — Real Numbers

slides.title: At the Railway Station
slides.storyContext: Raj is queuing for tickets at Delhi Railway Station. The station master Mr. Sharma is distributing 240 and 180 tickets equally among different counters. Raj wonders: what is the largest number of counters that can receive equal tickets?

image.alt: At the Railway Station — Real Numbers

slides.title: What Are Real Numbers?

points.label: Real Numbers
points.text: All numbers on the number line: natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rationals (fractions), and irrationals (like √2, π).

points.label: Examples
points.text: 5 (natural), 0 (whole), -3 (integer), 1/2 (rational), √7 (irrational)

points.label: Order Property
points.text: Real numbers can be compared: 2 < 5, -1 < 0, 0.5 > 0.4

slides.inSimpleWords: Real numbers are all the numbers you can place on a line, including whole numbers and fractions.

image.alt: What Are Real Numbers? — Real Numbers

slides.title: Euclid's Division Lemma

points.label: Definition
points.text: For any two positive integers a and b, there exist unique integers q and r such that a = bq + r, where 0 ≤ r < b.

slides.inSimpleWords: Dividing a larger number by a smaller one always leaves a remainder smaller than the divisor.

image.alt: Euclid's Division Lemma — Real Numbers

slides.title: Raj Helps the Station Master
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma tells Raj: 'I have 240 morning tickets and 180 evening tickets to distribute equally across counters. Each counter must get the same number of both types.' Raj realizes this is a divisibility problem! He needs to find the largest number that divides both 240 and 180.

image.alt: Raj Helps the Station Master — Real Numbers

points.label: HCF(240, 180) = 60
points.text: The station can use 60 counters, each getting 4 + 3 = 7 tickets total.

example.problem: Find HCF(455, 130)

image.alt: Finding HCF using Euclid's Algorithm — Real Numbers

example.problem: Find HCF(560, 210) using Euclid's Division Lemma

image.alt: Practice: Euclid's Algorithm Step-by-Step — Real Numbers

slides.title: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic

points.label: Theorem
points.text: Every integer greater than 1 is either prime or can be uniquely expressed as a product of primes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Any number can be broken into prime building blocks in only one way.

image.alt: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic — Real Numbers

slides.title: Prime Factorization at the Station
slides.storyContext: Priya joins Raj at the station. She asks Mr. Sharma: 'Can we also find HCF by breaking down the numbers into primes?' Mr. Sharma nods and Priya writes: 240 = 2⁴ × 3 × 5 and 180 = 2² × 3² × 5. They pick the smallest power of each common prime to find HCF = 2² × 3 × 5 = 60. Same answer!

image.alt: Prime Factorization at the Station — Real Numbers

example.problem: Prime factorize 84 and 126, then find HCF

image.alt: Prime Factorization Practice — Real Numbers

points.label: Formula
points.text: For any two numbers a and b: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b

example.problem: If HCF(12, 18) = 6, find LCM(12, 18)

image.alt: HCF × LCM Property — Real Numbers

example.problem: Two buses leave Delhi station together at 6 AM. Bus A returns every 90 minutes, Bus B every 150 minutes. When will both be at the station together again?
example.solution: Find LCM(90, 150). 90 = 2 × 3² × 5; 150 = 2 × 3 × 5². LCM = 2 × 3² × 5² = 450 minutes = 7.5 hours. Answer: 1:30 PM.

image.alt: Challenge: Bus Schedule (LCM Application) — Real Numbers

slides.title: Proving √2 is Irrational

points.label: Assume
points.text: √2 = p/q where p, q are coprime integers (HCF = 1)

points.label: Square
points.text: 2 = p²/q², so p² = 2q²

points.label: Conclusion
points.text: This means p² is even, so p is even. Let p = 2m. Then 4m² = 2q², so q² = 2m², making q even too.

points.label: Contradiction
points.text: Both p and q are even, contradicting our assumption they were coprime. Therefore √2 is irrational.

slides.inSimpleWords: √2 cannot be written as a fraction of two whole numbers.

image.alt: Proving √2 is Irrational — Real Numbers

slides.title: Priya's Puzzle About √2
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Raj a spiral drawn on paper. 'Can you measure this exactly?' she asks. 'This spiral is made of irrational numbers like √2. No matter how precise your ruler, you can never express √2 as a simple fraction. It's infinite and non-repeating!' Raj is amazed that some real numbers can't be fractions at all.

image.alt: Priya's Puzzle About √2 — Real Numbers

example.problem: Show that √3 is irrational (by contradiction)
example.solution: Assume √3 = p/q (coprime). Then 3 = p²/q², so p² = 3q². This means p² is divisible by 3, so p is divisible by 3. Let p = 3k. Then 9k² = 3q², so q² = 3k², meaning q is also divisible by 3. Contradiction! So √3 is irrational.

image.alt: Irrationality Proof Practice — Real Numbers

points.label: Terminating
points.text: 1/8 = 0.125 (ends after 3 decimal places)

points.label: Non-Terminating Repeating
points.text: 1/3 = 0.333... (repeats forever)

points.label: Rule
points.text: p/q is terminating if q = 2^a × 5^b (only factors 2 and 5)

example.problem: Is 7/80 terminating or repeating?

image.alt: Decimal Expansions: Terminating and Non-Terminating — Real Numbers

example.problem: Write 13/40 as a decimal and determine if it's terminating.
example.solution: 40 = 2³ × 5¹ (only factors 2 and 5), so 13/40 terminates. 13/40 = 0.325

image.alt: Decimal Expansion Practice — Real Numbers

example.problem: For each fraction, say if it's terminating or repeating: (a) 5/16 (b) 7/15 (c) 9/24
example.solution: (a) 16 = 2⁴, so terminating: 0.3125. (b) 15 = 3 × 5 (has factor 3), so repeating: 0.4666... (c) 24 = 2³ × 3 (has factor 3), so repeating. But 9/24 = 3/8, and 8 = 2³, so 0.375 terminates.

image.alt: Challenge: Classify Decimal Types — Real Numbers

slides.title: Mr. Sharma's Final Lesson
slides.storyContext: As Raj leaves the station, Mr. Sharma reflects: 'You see, ticket numbers, bus schedules, prime factorization—they all hide the same mathematical truth. Real numbers order everything in the world. Divisibility is the language of fairness: dividing things equally. And some numbers, like √2, remind us that reality is deeper than simple fractions.' Raj nods, understanding now that mathematics isn't abstract—it's everywhere.

image.alt: Mr. Sharma's Final Lesson — Real Numbers

example.problem: The station master needs to pack 48 mathematics books and 36 science books into identical kits with no books left over. What is the maximum number of kits?
example.solution: Find HCF(48, 36). 48 = 36 × 1 + 12; 36 = 12 × 3 + 0. HCF = 12 kits. Each kit has 48/12 = 4 math books and 36/12 = 3 science books.

image.alt: Solved Problem: Railway Ticket Distribution — Real Numbers

example.problem: Two buses leave a station together at 8 AM. Bus A returns every 120 minutes and Bus B every 180 minutes. When will both buses be at the station together again?
example.solution: Find LCM(120, 180). 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5; 180 = 2² × 3² × 5. LCM = 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360 minutes = 6 hours. Answer: 2 PM.

image.alt: Your Turn: Bus Schedule Problem — Real Numbers

slides.title: Rational and Irrational Numbers on the Number Line

points.label: Rational Numbers
points.text: Numbers expressible as p/q (fractions). Example: 1/2, 3/4, -5/3, 0, 7

points.label: Irrational Numbers
points.text: Cannot be expressed as p/q. Example: √2, √3, π, e. Decimal form never terminates or repeats.

points.label: Together
points.text: Rationals and irrationals together form all real numbers, densely filling the entire number line.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real numbers are all rational fractions plus irrational numbers like √2.

image.alt: Rational and Irrational Numbers on the Number Line — Real Numbers

slides.title: Mixed Problems: HCF and LCM Together

example.problem: Two ropes of lengths 60 cm and 90 cm. Cut them into equal pieces with no wastage. Max piece length? How many pieces total?
example.solution: Max length = HCF(60, 90). 60 = 2²×3×5; 90 = 2×3²×5. HCF = 2×3×5 = 30 cm/piece. Total pieces = 60/30 + 90/30 = 2 + 3 = 5 pieces.

image.alt: Mixed Problems: HCF and LCM Together — Real Numbers

example.problem: A school has 504 blue chairs and 392 green chairs. Arrange them in rows with same count of each color, max chairs/row. How many rows?
example.solution: Find HCF(504, 392). 504 = 2³×3²×7; 392 = 2³×7². HCF = 2³×7 = 56 chairs/row. Blue rows: 504/56 = 9. Green rows: 392/56 = 7. Total rows = 16.

image.alt: Challenge: Real-World Divisibility — Real Numbers

example.problem: What do √2, √3, √5, √7 have in common? Are all of them irrational?
example.solution: Yes, √p is irrational for any prime p. Proof: if √p = a/b (coprime), then p = a²/b², so a² = pb², meaning p divides a. Let a = pm. Then p²m² = pb², so pm² = b², meaning p divides b. Contradiction, so √p is irrational.

image.alt: Irrational Sequences and Patterns — Real Numbers

points.text: Real numbers include rationals (fractions) and irrationals (like √2)
Euclid's Division Lemma: a = bq + r (0 ≤ r < b)
HCF (GCD) found using Euclid's algorithm or prime factorization
Fundamental Theorem: every number is a unique product of primes
HCF × LCM = product of two numbers
√2 is irrational (cannot be written as p/q)
p/q terminates only if denominator has only factors 2 and 5

subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's Garden Design
hook: A student uses polynomials to design the perfect garden layout.

image.alt: Polynomials: Roots and Factors — Polynomials

slides.title: Designing a Rectangular Garden
slides.storyContext: Priya's grandmother has 50 meters of fencing. Priya wants to design a rectangular garden where the area is maximized. She writes: Area = x(25 - x). Arjun says this is a polynomial!

image.alt: Designing a Rectangular Garden — Polynomials

slides.title: Polynomial Definition and Degree

points.label: Definition
points.text: A polynomial in x is p(x) = a₀ + a₁x + a₂x² + ... + aₙxⁿ where coefficients are real numbers and n is a non-negative integer.

points.label: Degree
points.text: The highest power of x. Example: p(x) = 2x³ + 5x - 3 has degree 3.

points.label: Types
points.text: Linear (degree 1), Quadratic (degree 2), Cubic (degree 3)

slides.inSimpleWords: A polynomial is an expression with x raised to various powers, combined with numbers.

image.alt: Polynomial Definition and Degree — Polynomials

slides.title: Priya Discovers Polynomial Form
slides.storyContext: Priya writes out her garden equation: if the length is x and the width is (25 - x), then Area = x(25 - x) = 25x - x². She realizes she can expand this—it becomes -x² + 25x + 0. Arjun points out: 'This is a degree-2 polynomial, or quadratic! Every term is a power of x multiplied by a number.'

image.alt: Priya Discovers Polynomial Form — Polynomials

points.label: Definition
points.text: A value r is a zero of p(x) if p(r) = 0.

points.label: Example
points.text: For p(x) = x² - 5x + 6, if x = 2: p(2) = 4 - 10 + 6 = 0. So 2 is a zero.

example.problem: Find a zero of p(x) = x² - 9
example.solution: p(3) = 9 - 9 = 0. So x = 3 is a zero. Also x = -3.

image.alt: Zeros of a Polynomial — Polynomials

slides.title: Garden Zeros: When Area Becomes Zero
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'When is the area zero?' She writes 25x - x² = 0 and factors: x(25 - x) = 0. So x = 0 or x = 25. She realizes: if the length is 0 or 25, there's no garden! The zeros tell us boundary values where the garden collapses.

image.alt: Garden Zeros: When Area Becomes Zero — Polynomials

example.problem: Find the zeros of p(x) = x² + 3x + 2

image.alt: Finding Zeros by Factoring — Polynomials

slides.title: Remainder Theorem

points.label: Theorem
points.text: If polynomial p(x) is divided by (x - a), the remainder is p(a).

points.label: Example
points.text: Divide p(x) = x³ - 2x² + 5 by (x - 1). Remainder = p(1) = 1 - 2 + 5 = 4

slides.inSimpleWords: When dividing a polynomial by (x - a), just plug in a to get the remainder.

image.alt: Remainder Theorem — Polynomials

example.problem: Find the remainder when p(x) = 2x³ + 3x² - x + 5 is divided by (x - 2)
example.solution: By Remainder Theorem, remainder = p(2) = 2(8) + 3(4) - 2 + 5 = 16 + 12 - 2 + 5 = 31

image.alt: Practice: Remainder Theorem — Polynomials

points.label: Theorem
points.text: (x - a) is a factor of p(x) if and only if p(a) = 0.

points.label: Example
points.text: Is (x - 2) a factor of p(x) = x³ - 4x² + 5x - 2? Check: p(2) = 8 - 16 + 10 - 2 = 0. Yes!

example.problem: Show (x + 1) is a factor of p(x) = x³ + 2x² - x - 2

image.alt: Factor Theorem — Polynomials

slides.title: Finding Factors in the Garden
slides.storyContext: Arjun says: 'Your polynomial 25x - x² factors as x(25 - x). Let's check: are x = 0 and x = 25 zeros?' Priya plugs in: 'Yes! So (x - 0) and (x - 25) are factors.' Arjun smiles: 'Because zeros are zeros, the factors are linear terms (x - zero).' This is the Factor Theorem in action.

image.alt: Finding Factors in the Garden — Polynomials

slides.title: Factorization of Quadratic Polynomials

points.label: Method
points.text: For ax² + bx + c, find two numbers whose product is ac and sum is b.

points.label: Example
points.text: x² + 7x + 12: two numbers are 3 and 4 (3×4=12, 3+4=7). So x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4)

slides.inSimpleWords: Break a quadratic into two simple factors.

image.alt: Factorization of Quadratic Polynomials — Polynomials

example.problem: Factorize 2x² + 5x + 3
example.solution: Here a=2, b=5, c=3. Product ac = 6. Find two numbers: 2 and 3 (2+3=5, 2×3=6). Split: 2x² + 2x + 3x + 3 = 2x(x+1) + 3(x+1) = (2x+3)(x+1)

image.alt: Factorize Quadratics: Step-by-Step — Polynomials

example.problem: Factorize: (a) x² + 8x + 15 (b) 3x² - 10x + 8
example.solution: (a) Find two numbers: 3 and 5 (sum 8, product 15). So (x+3)(x+5). (b) Product ac=24. Numbers: 4 and 6 (sum 10, product 24). 3x² - 4x - 6x + 8 = x(3x-4) - 2(3x-4) = (x-2)(3x-4)

image.alt: Challenge: Factor Quadratics — Polynomials

points.label: Formula
points.text: Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder

points.label: Example
points.text: Divide 2x² + 5x + 2 by x + 2. Quotient = 2x + 1, Remainder = 0. So 2x² + 5x + 2 = (x + 2)(2x + 1)

image.alt: Division Algorithm for Polynomials — Polynomials

example.problem: Divide x³ - 6x² + 11x - 6 by (x - 1)
example.solution: Using synthetic division or long division: x³ - 6x² + 11x - 6 = (x-1)(x² - 5x + 6) = (x-1)(x-2)(x-3). Remainder = 0.

image.alt: Polynomial Long Division — Polynomials

slides.title: Mrs. Gupta's Garden Flourishes
slides.storyContext: Using polynomials, Priya finds that maximum area occurs at x = 12.5 meters (the vertex of the parabola). Mrs. Gupta sets up the garden with length 12.5m and width 12.5m—a square! It gives 156.25 m² of space. 'Polynomials made my garden perfect!' Mrs. Gupta exclaims.

image.alt: Mrs. Gupta's Garden Flourishes — Polynomials

example.problem: Priya's garden area is A(x) = x(25 - x) = 25x - x². What are the zeros? When is area maximized?
example.solution: Zeros: 25x - x² = 0 → x(25 - x) = 0 → x = 0 or x = 25. Maximum at vertex x = 12.5 meters, giving A = 156.25 m².

image.alt: Priya's Garden Area — Polynomials

slides.title: Graphing Polynomials: Shape and Behavior

points.label: Degree 2 (Quadratic)
points.text: U-shaped parabola (opens up if a > 0, down if a < 0)

points.label: Degree 3 (Cubic)
points.text: S-shaped curve, crosses x-axis at up to 3 points

points.label: Zeros as Intercepts
points.text: Zeros are x-intercepts where the graph touches or crosses the x-axis

slides.inSimpleWords: Higher-degree polynomials have more wiggles; zeros are where the curve hits the x-axis.

image.alt: Graphing Polynomials: Shape and Behavior — Polynomials

example.problem: Factorize 2x³ - x² - 5x + 2 completely (if possible)
example.solution: Test rational roots using rational root theorem. After testing: (2x-1)(x² - (x-2)) doesn't work cleanly. Try factoring by grouping or using synthetic division with likely roots. Answer: (2x-1) is a factor if 2(1/8)-(1/4)-5(1/2)+2=0, which requires verification.

image.alt: Complete Factorization — Polynomials

example.problem: Find all zeros of p(x) = x³ - 6x² + 11x - 6
example.solution: Test x = 1: 1 - 6 + 11 - 6 = 0 ✓. So (x-1) is a factor. Divide: (x-1)(x²-5x+6) = (x-1)(x-2)(x-3). Zeros: x = 1, 2, 3

image.alt: Cubic Polynomial Zeros — Polynomials

example.problem: Without dividing, prove (x-3) is a factor of p(x) = x³ - 9x² + 26x - 24
example.solution: Use Factor Theorem: p(3) = 27 - 81 + 78 - 24 = 0. So (x-3) is a factor.

image.alt: Challenge: Prove It's a Factor — Polynomials

example.problem: A shop's profit is P(x) = -x² + 40x - 300, where x = items sold (hundreds). Find break-even points.
example.solution: -x² + 40x - 300 = 0. Divide by -1: x² - 40x + 300 = 0. Discriminant = 1600 - 1200 = 400. x = (40 ± 20)/2 = 30 or 10. Break-even at 1000 or 3000 items.

image.alt: Polynomial Applications in Business — Polynomials

slides.title: Maximum Garden Height
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Gupta asks: 'If I plant flowers in rows, with each row 1 meter apart, how tall should they be to fill the space perfectly?' This leads to optimizing a polynomial h(x) = -0.1x² + 3x, where x is distance. The maximum tells us the perfect height.

image.alt: Maximum Garden Height — Polynomials

example.problem: For ax² + bx + c with roots r₁ and r₂, show that r₁ + r₂ = -b/a and r₁ × r₂ = c/a
example.solution: If r₁, r₂ are roots: a(x-r₁)(x-r₂) = ax² - a(r₁+r₂)x + ar₁r₂. Comparing: -a(r₁+r₂) = b, so r₁+r₂ = -b/a. And ar₁r₂ = c, so r₁r₂ = c/a.

image.alt: Vieta's Formulas for Quadratics — Polynomials

points.text: Polynomial: sum of terms with variables raised to whole number powers
Zero: a value where p(x) = 0, also an x-intercept on the graph
Remainder Theorem: remainder when dividing by (x - a) is p(a)
Factor Theorem: (x - a) is a factor iff p(a) = 0
Quadratic factorization: find two numbers with product ac and sum b
Complete factorization breaks polynomial into linear factors (x - zero)
Graphs of quadratics are parabolas; zeros are where curve crosses x-axis

subject: Mathematics
chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
title: Rohit and Neha's Coffee Shop Plan
hook: Two friends plan to open a cafe and need math to figure out prices and quantities.

slides.title: Pair of Linear Equations: Graphical and Algebraic Solutions

image.alt: Pair of Linear Equations: Graphical and Algebraic Solutions — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: Opening a Coffee Shop
slides.storyContext: Rohit and Neha want to open a small cafe in Bangalore. They can spend ₹50,000 on equipment and supplies. Coffee makers cost ₹5,000 each and grinders cost ₹3,000 each. They want 6 items total. How many of each should they buy?

image.alt: Opening a Coffee Shop — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: Linear Equation in Two Variables

points.label: Definition
points.text: An equation of the form ax + by + c = 0, where a, b, c are real numbers and a, b ≠ 0.

points.label: Example
points.text: Number of items: x + y = 6 (where x = coffee makers, y = grinders)

points.label: Solution
points.text: Any pair (x, y) satisfying the equation. For x + y = 6: (1, 5), (2, 4), (3, 3), etc.

slides.inSimpleWords: An equation with two variables forms a straight line when graphed.

image.alt: Linear Equation in Two Variables — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: Setting Up Two Equations
slides.storyContext: Rohit writes two equations from the requirements: 'We need 6 items total: x + y = 6. We have ₹50,000 budget: 5000x + 3000y = 50000. These are two linear equations with two unknowns!' Neha asks: 'So we need to find x and y that work in BOTH equations?' 'Exactly!' Rohit replies.

image.alt: Setting Up Two Equations — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: System of Linear Equations

points.label: Definition
points.text: Two equations: 5000x + 3000y = 50000 (money) and x + y = 6 (count)

points.label: Solution
points.text: The pair (x, y) that satisfies BOTH equations simultaneously.

points.label: Simplified
points.text: Divide first by 1000: 5x + 3y = 50 and x + y = 6

slides.inSimpleWords: Find values of x and y that work in both equations at the same time.

image.alt: System of Linear Equations — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: Substitution Method

points.label: Step 1
points.text: From x + y = 6, express y = 6 - x

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Substitute in 5x + 3y = 50: 5x + 3(6 - x) = 50

points.label: Wait
points.text: x = 16 but x + y = 6? This means they can't buy only 6 items for ₹50,000 at these prices.

slides.inSimpleWords: Solve one equation for one variable, then substitute into the other.

image.alt: Substitution Method — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Solve: 2x + y = 7 and x - y = 2
example.solution: From second: x = y + 2. Substitute into first: 2(y + 2) + y = 7 → 2y + 4 + y = 7 → 3y = 3 → y = 1. Then x = 1 + 2 = 3. Solution: (3, 1)

image.alt: Substitution Method: Step-by-Step — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Given: 5x + 3y = 50 and x + y = 6

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Multiply second by 3: 3x + 3y = 18

example.problem: Solve: 2x + y = 7 and x - y = 2
example.solution: Add: 3x = 9 → x = 3. Substitute: 3 - y = 2 → y = 1. Solution: (3, 1)

image.alt: Elimination Method — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Solve: 3x + 2y = 13 and 5x - 3y = 1
example.solution: Multiply first by 3: 9x + 6y = 39. Multiply second by 2: 10x - 6y = 2. Add: 19x = 41 → x = 41/19. Substitute back to find y = (13 - 3(41/19))/2.

image.alt: Elimination Method Practice — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

points.label: Unique Solution
points.text: Lines intersect at one point (a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂). Example: 2x + 3y = 12 and x - y = 1

points.label: No Solution
points.text: Lines are parallel (a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂). Example: x + y = 5 and x + y = 10

points.label: Infinite Solutions
points.text: Lines are identical (a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂). Example: 2x + 4y = 6 and x + 2y = 3

image.alt: Types of Solutions — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: A Problem Emerges
slides.storyContext: Mr. Patel the accountant rechecks Rohit and Neha's numbers. 'Your system has no solution,' he says. 'With 6 items costing ₹50,000, the cheapest option (all grinders at 3000 each) costs ₹18,000. The most expensive (all coffee makers) costs ₹30,000. You can't hit ₹50,000 exactly!' The friends realize they need to adjust either the budget or the item count.

image.alt: A Problem Emerges — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: Graphical Method

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Plot both lines on a coordinate grid.

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Find the point where lines intersect.

points.label: Example
points.text: For x + y = 6: passes through (0, 6) and (6, 0). For 5x + 3y = 50: passes through (0, 16.67) and (10, 0)

slides.inSimpleWords: Graph both equations and see where the lines cross.

image.alt: Graphical Method — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Solve graphically: x + y = 5 and 2x - y = 1
example.solution: Plot x + y = 5: (0,5), (5,0). Plot 2x - y = 1: (0,-1), (1,3). Lines intersect at (2, 3). Solution: x = 2, y = 3. Check: 2+3=5 ✓ and 2(2)-3=1 ✓

image.alt: Graphical Solution Example — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Solve: x + y = 3 and x + y = 5
example.solution: Both lines have the form x + y = constant. They are parallel (same slope). They never intersect, so NO SOLUTION. The system is inconsistent.

image.alt: Challenge: When Lines Are Parallel — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

slides.title: Rohit and Neha Adjust Their Plan
slides.storyContext: Rohit proposes a new budget: ₹32,000 instead of ₹50,000. With x + y = 5 items and 5000x + 3000y = 32000 (simplified: 5x + 3y = 32). Let's solve. From first: y = 5 - x. Substitute: 5x + 3(5-x) = 32 → 5x + 15 - 3x = 32 → 2x = 17 → x = 8.5. Still not a whole number. After more discussion, they settle on: 3 espresso machines and 2 milk frothers for ₹21,000.

image.alt: Rohit and Neha Adjust Their Plan — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Revised: Rohit and Neha want to buy espresso machines (₹8,000 each) and milk frothers (₹2,000 each) totaling ₹32,000 and 5 items. How many of each?
example.solution: Equations: 8x + 2y = 32 (divide by 2: 4x + y = 16) and x + y = 5. From second: y = 5 - x. Substitute: 4x + (5 - x) = 16 → 3x = 11 → x = 11/3 ≈ 3.67. Not whole. Adjust to 8x + 2y = 30 and x + y = 5: y = 5 - x → 8x + 2(5 - x) = 30 → 6x = 20 → x = 10/3. Real solution: 3 espresso + 2 frothers = ₹28,000.

example.problem: At a vegetable market, Priya buys 2 kg of tomatoes and 3 kg of onions for ₹170. Neha buys 1 kg of tomatoes and 2 kg of onions for ₹100. Find the price per kg of each.
example.solution: Let x = price of tomato/kg, y = price of onion/kg. Equations: 2x + 3y = 170 and x + 2y = 100. From second: x = 100 - 2y. Substitute: 2(100 - 2y) + 3y = 170 → 200 - 4y + 3y = 170 → y = 30. Then x = 100 - 60 = 40. Tomatoes ₹40/kg, onions ₹30/kg.

slides.title: When to Use Each Method

points.label: Substitution
points.text: Best when one equation is already solved for a variable, or one coefficient is 1.

points.label: Elimination
points.text: Best when coefficients are easy to make equal by multiplying.

points.label: Graphical
points.text: Best to visualize solutions; clearly shows if lines intersect, are parallel, or coincide.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different methods work better for different equations; pick based on what's easiest.

example.problem: Solve: 4x + 6y = 8 and 2x + 3y = 4
example.solution: Note: 4x + 6y = 8 is 2(2x + 3y) = 2(4), so it's the same as 2x + 3y = 4. The two equations represent the same line! Infinite solutions of form (x, (4-2x)/3) for any x.

image.alt: Challenge: Infinite Solutions — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.solution: Multiply first by 6: 3x + 2y = 12. Multiply second by 4: x + 2y = 4. Subtract: 2x = 8 → x = 4. Then 2y = 4 - 4 = 0 → y = 0. Solution: (4, 0)

image.alt: Fraction Coefficients in Systems — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: What does the system tell us? 3x + 4y = 12 and 6x + 8y = 24
example.solution: Second equation = 2 × First equation. They represent the same line! Infinitely many solutions: (x, (12-3x)/4) for any x. The system is dependent.

image.alt: Challenge: Dependent Equations — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Asha is twice as old as Priya. In 3 years, their ages will sum to 45. Find current ages.
example.solution: Let A = Asha's age, P = Priya's age. A = 2P and (A+3) + (P+3) = 45. Substitute: (2P+3) + (P+3) = 45 → 3P + 6 = 45 → 3P = 39 → P = 13. Then A = 26. Asha is 26, Priya is 13.

image.alt: Real-Life System: Age Problem — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Solve using comparison: 3x - y = 5 and 2x + y = 10
example.solution: From first: y = 3x - 5. From second: y = 10 - 2x. Set equal: 3x - 5 = 10 - 2x → 5x = 15 → x = 3. Then y = 10 - 6 = 4. Solution: (3, 4)

slides.title: Cafe Opening Day
slides.storyContext: With 3 espresso machines and 2 frothers in place, Rohit and Neha open the cafe. They charge ₹50 per espresso and ₹30 per coffee. After day 1, they earned ₹4,500 from 120 drinks total. How many of each did they sell? This is a real system they must solve!

image.alt: Cafe Opening Day — Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables

example.problem: Solve: 50e + 30c = 4500 (revenue) and e + c = 120 (total drinks)
example.solution: From second: c = 120 - e. Substitute: 50e + 30(120 - e) = 4500 → 50e + 3600 - 30e = 4500 → 20e = 900 → e = 45. Then c = 75. They sold 45 espressos and 75 coffees.

points.text: Linear equation in 2 variables: ax + by + c = 0 (straight line)
System: two equations where both must be satisfied simultaneously
Substitution method: solve one for a variable, substitute in other
Elimination method: multiply to make coefficients equal, then subtract
Three types: unique solution (lines intersect), no solution (parallel), infinite (same line)
Graphical method: plot both lines and find intersection point
Real-world problems often require checking if solutions are whole numbers and make practical sense
